chunks: "Internal resistance is the opposition inside the battery to current flow.
The simplest model is an ideal voltage source, the open-circuit voltage, in series with a resistor, so the terminal voltage is the open-circuit voltage minus current times that resistance.

It matters because it makes the voltage sag under load, it wastes power as heat, I squared R, it limits the maximum current and power the battery can deliver, and it makes state-of-charge estimates from voltage wrong under load.
For a LiPo it's typically tens of milliohms for a phone cell. It isn't a constant.

With temperature it rises sharply in the cold, because the ions move more slowly and the reactions slow down: at zero degrees it might be two to three times the room-temperature value, and several times higher at minus twenty.
With aging it increases as the SEI layer grows and contacts degrade, perhaps doubling by end of life. It also depends on state of charge, getting worse when nearly empty.

And with frequency: at high frequency you only see the ohmic part, the electrolyte and contacts, so a 1 kilohertz meter reads lower than the DC resistance you'd get from a ten-second pulse, which includes charge transfer and diffusion.
So you model it as a resistor plus a couple of parallel R-C pairs."
